transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Asha (Redwood AE), Tom (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood), Marta (Aperture), Liam (Aperture SRE), Priya (Aperture CTO), Noah (Aperture ML)

[00:00] Asha: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. we wanted to run through throughput tuning best practices - continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, and token limits especially for VPC/private infra. quick intros?
[00:15] Marta: Hi, Marta here, engineering manager on the ML infra team at Aperture.
[00:22] Liam: Liam, SRE, I'll be running the VMs and the k8s side.
[00:27] Priya: Priya, CTO, listening in for architecture and compliance questions.
[00:33] Tom: Tom Nguyen, Redwood SE. Diego and I will do the deep dive.
[00:40] Noah: Noah, ML engineer, will share load patterns.

[01:05] Tom: Okay great. quick overview: continuous batching is our recommended mode for high throughput workloads that have variable request arrival — it keeps the scheduler filling batches rather than waiting for fixed-size windows. the tradeoff is a small latency tail but huge cost benefits.
[01:40] Marta: can you explain scheduler knobs? we saw a config field called max_num_seqs and some backpressure settings in the docs but not sure how they map to our traffic.
[02:00] Tom: absolutely. so the main knobs are: max_batch_tokens, max_num_seqs (max concurrent sequences in a batch), max_wait_ms (how long scheduler will wait to fill the batch), and continuous_batching_enabled flag. The runtime also has a burst_capacity for short spikes.
[02:25] Diego: I'll add: on GPU we try to target a token budget that's friendly to the attention kernels. e.g., on A100 with our quantized fp16 path we hit best throughput with batch token budgets around 32k-64k tokens depending on sequence length distribution.
[02:48] Liam: hmm, our distribution is bimodal — a lot of short queries ~20-50 tokens and a tail of long summaries ~800-1k tokens. is continuous batching still good?
[03:05] Tom: yes, continuous batching helps a lot for that pattern. you want to tune max_num_seqs to avoid packing too many short sequences which can blow past token budget if a long request arrives. set max_num_seqs to cap concurrency per batch for fairness. for example, start with max_num_seqs=64, max_batch_tokens=32000, max_wait_ms=15.
[03:35] Marta: Why 15ms? sounds low.
[03:40] Tom: it's a small wait to get extra requests in but still keeps p50 latency tight. you can increase to 30-50ms if your SLO allows slightly higher p50 but can significantly improve consumed tokens and throughput.
[04:05] Priya: Are there any gotchas for VPC or on-prem installs? we run in a private VPC with strict networking and no internet egress.
[04:14] Diego: main considerations: KV cache benefits are local — ensure the cache persistence path is on fast NVMe, and for multi-node setups use our routing policy to favor warm cache nodes. avoid making cache writes synchronous across nodes as that will add latency.
[04:36] Noah: Quick Q: how does KV cache interact with continuous batching when some requests hit cached prefixes and others don't?
[04:44] Tom: good question. if a request hits a prefix cache, the runtime can short-circuit some attention compute for those tokens, which reduces token cost for that request. scheduler measures expected compute per-seq and will still pack mixed cached/uncached sequences but we recommend having a separate low-latency route for mostly-cached workloads.
[05:10] Liam: our SRE is worried about OOM spikes when long sequences get packed with high max_num_seqs. any safe defaults to prevent that?
[05:20] Diego: use max_num_seqs to cap the number of sequences, and also set a per-sequence max_token_limit. e.g., max_sequence_tokens=1024 to reject or route very long requests to a separate pool. we also have soft limits that abort batch if the aggregate token budget would exceed GPU memory.
[05:48] Asha: also note the scheduler has a max_batch_tokens_hard_limit which will prevent OOM by refusing the batch rather than sending it to the GPU. we prefer graceful rejection or routing to a long-runner pool.

[06:10] Tom: example we gave another customer: short Q&A median 40 tokens, occasional 1k token doc write. They used two pools: pool A continuous batching tuned for short queries, pool B dedicated for long seqs with lower batch size and higher max_wait_ms. that isolates latency and avoids OOM.
[06:38] Marta: That seems likely for us. do you have recommended yaml snippets?
[06:44] Tom: yes I'll share. quick pseudocode:
- continuous_batching_enabled: true
- max_wait_ms: 20
- max_num_seqs: 64
- max_batch_tokens: 32000
- max_sequence_tokens: 1024
- routing: route-long-seqs-to: pool-long

[07:10] Noah: about quantization — we run A100s and are thinking about 4-bit quantization. any accuracy cost vs perf tradeoffs at serving?
[07:20] Diego: 4-bit works great for many instruct-style models; latency and token throughput improve a bunch. but you might see small drops on edge-case reasoning tasks. we recommend running a small eval set during the POC. Redwood Optimize can suggest a quantization profile per-model.
[07:45] Priya: security question: if we enable KV cache persistence and use it on VPC, are tokens or customer data persisted in plaintext?
[07:56] Tom: no, cache keys and any persisted artifacts are encrypted at rest using the KMS you provide in the private deployment. we also support HSM-backed KMS for enterprise. logs that include user-visible prompts are redacted by default but can be configured.

[08:30] Marta: about scheduler knobs again — what about backpressure? we saw a parameter called overload_threshold.
[08:38] Tom: overload_threshold toggles how the scheduler signals backpressure to the front-end; typical setting is 0.8 to start, which means when GPU token budget usage hits 80% the scheduler starts shedding or routing less-latency-critical requests. it prevents sudden latency spikes.
[08:58] Liam: will the shedding be per-route? we need priority routing between interactive UI calls and batch analytics calls.
[09:06] Tom: yes, you configure priority per route; interactive routes get higher priority and are routed to a reserve capacity or lower batch token pool. analytics or low-priority jobs can be routed to a cheaper, high-batch pool.

[09:30] Marta: any tips on measuring the right max_num_seqs?
[09:36] Diego: collect sequence-length histogram and request interarrival times. A simple heuristic: max_num_seqs = desired_concurrency / (average_seq_length / target_seq_length_unit). but simpler: run the benchmark with autoscaler disabled, try values 32,64,128 and watch p50/p95/p99 and GPU utilization.
[10:00] Noah: we can dump the histogram, will share it.

[10:20] Tom: For token limits: set per-route max_tokens and also overall per-request hard limit. if users hit hard limit return 413-style error and optionally route to a larger-capacity pool.
[10:40] Priya: how do we monitor KV cache hit rates and their effect on cost?
[10:48] Tom: Console exposes cache hit metrics and token-equivalent-savings. we show a per-route cost breakdown that attributes saved tokens to cache hits. for private deployments the same metrics are available via Prometheus endpoints.

[11:15] Marta: we heard about continuous batching causing jitter in latency — any mitigations?
[11:22] Diego: tune max_wait_ms and use latency SLO reserve capacity; also set a p95-target autoscaling policy to spin up instances before the tail degrades. an alternative is latency-first pooling for the UI path.

[11:45] Liam: what about model variants — routing fallback to smaller quantized model when overloaded?
[11:52] Tom: yes, Redwood supports automatic fallback to cheaper variants based on policy. you can define model fallback chains with thresholds on latency and errors. it's common: primary is full-precision model, fallback is quantized or smaller family.

[12:20] Marta: can you walk through the benchmark plan you mentioned?
[12:25] Tom: sure. Redwood will run a 2-hour benchmark using your sample traffic profile. we spin up a dedicated pool in the private env (or we can run on Redwood infra if you prefer), sweep max_num_seqs [32,64,128], max_wait_ms [10,20,50], and measure p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1k-tokens. we'll also run with and without kv-cache warm to show delta.
[12:55] Priya: If you run the benchmark inside our VPC, we'll need an MOU and limited access — security team will review.
[13:04] Asha: understood, we'll share a minimal access plan and a security checklist.

[13:20] Noah: small note — our tail requests can be multi-segment with back-and-forth, should we use streaming response or non-streamed for caching benefits?
[13:30] Tom: streaming yields lower perceived latency for users but complicates some caching semantics; for multi-turn chats with KV caching of prefixes, non-streamed with prefix cache can be more effective. you can hybridize: stream for interactive short queries, then non-stream for longer generation tasks.

[14:05] Marta: any specific kernel/driver versions we should pin on A100s?
[14:12] Diego: for best perf use CUDA 12.x and driver matching recommended by our runtime docs; also use NCCL 2.17+ for multi-GPU. quantized kernels have specific cuBLAS/cuDNN dependencies which we'll list in the config we send.

[14:35] Liam: autoscaling — is continuous batching impacted when nodes scale up/down rapidly?
[14:42] Tom: yes, frequent scale events can cause cache warm-up churn; prefer scale-up thresholds that are coarse with predictive signals or use horizontal partitioning by route to avoid thrash. we recommend a cooldown of at least 2-3 minutes for heavy workloads.

[15:05] Marta: ok can we summarize concrete starting config for us?
[15:10] Tom: start with two pools:
- pool-interactive: continuous_batching_enabled=true, max_wait_ms=20, max_num_seqs=64, max_batch_tokens=32000, priority=high
- pool-long: continuous_batching_enabled=false, max_wait_ms=100, max_num_seqs=8, max_batch_tokens=8192, priority=low
Also set max_sequence_tokens=1024 route-level token limit and overload_threshold=0.8 and reserve 1 GPU for high-priority traffic.

[15:45] Priya: that seems reasonable. what's the typical cost delta when using quantized fallback?
[15:52] Diego: quantized (4-bit) variants can be 30-50% cheaper per-token and also reduce latency on some kernels. exact numbers depend on model size and the kernel backend. benchmark will show the delta.

[16:15] Asha: next steps recap — Tom will send scheduler yaml + example, Diego will include quantization notes and kernel deps, Asha will coordinate benchmark, Aperture to share traffic profile and any compliance constraints.
[16:33] Marta: we'll prepare the sample distribution and share by 4/22.
[16:40] Liam: security will need the access plan, we'll get that to you by 4/21.

[16:55] Tom: any other Qs?
[17:00] Priya: one more — for on-prem air-gapped option do you support offline model packaging?
[17:07] Diego: yes, we have an on-prem bundle and can do an offline install. it includes the runtime and compiled kernels; KMS integration is via bring-your-own-HSM. we may need to sign an NDA for model artifacts.

[17:30] Asha: great, thanks everyone. we'll share notes and the config; expect a follow-up with the benchmark invite.
[17:40] Marta: thanks team.
[17:45] Meeting end.
questions: How should we set max_num_seqs for bimodal sequence length distribution?
What are safe defaults to prevent OOM spikes?

notes: Redwood to run 2h benchmark inside Aperture VPC or on Redwood infra per preference.
Set per-route token limits and overload_threshold to 0.8.
